title: Family Nitnem
tomorrow: Fateh asks why he has to learn Punjabi. what does Simran say?

lines: DOES IT COUNT IF HALF ARE ASLEEP?
cards: The answer to who falls asleep: Harjit. Four minutes in. Simran's idea was simple: her own family, together, for Kirtan Sohila at bedtime, every night this week.
Bebe said yes before she finished the sentence. Fateh, sleeping over, demanded a cushion.
And her dad, home from a long day at the yard, sat down on the floor, leaned against the couch, and was gently snoring by the second hymn. Bebe kept reading.
Afterward Simran asked her: does it still count if half the family's asleep?

teach.b: Nitnem means the daily rule: the banis a Sikh reads each day. The Sikh code names them by time: Japji and others at dawn, Rehras at sunset, Kirtan Sohila before sleep. Each Sikh keeps their own.
A family Nitnem is simply keeping some of it together, even briefly. And Sohila opens, on ang 12, with a picture of exactly that.

teach.h: ANG 12: THE HOUSE WHERE PRAISE IS SUNG.
teach.b: In paraphrase, Guru Nanak says: in the house where the Creator's praise is sung and reflected on, in that house, sing the songs of praise. A house, not a temple.
Bebe's answer to Simran: the hymn doesn't say everyone in the house stays awake. It says the praise is sung there. Here's a neighbor who knows this rhythm.

teach.h: THE SHEMA: LYING DOWN, RISING UP.
teach.b: In the Torah, scripture for Jews, the Shema tells parents to keep God's words in their mouths at home, and to speak of them, in the words of the JPS 1917 translation, "when thou liest down, and when thou risest up."
Some Jewish families say the Shema with their children at bedtime. Two traditions, each in its own words, putting prayer at the edges of the day, at home.

teach.h: ONE DIFFERENCE: WHOSE CHARGE IT IS.
teach.b: One honest difference: the Shema's charge is spoken to parents, to teach these words diligently unto their children.
Nitnem is each Sikh's own daily discipline; a family can share it, but every person keeps their own.

how: Sikhs keep Nitnem, daily banis at dawn, sunset and bedtime; some families read Rehras or Kirtan Sohila together at home, often from a gutka, while each person also keeps their own.

o: a rule that only parents read the daily prayers
a yearly family prayer held at the gurdwara
keeping some of the daily banis together at home

Deuteronomy, in the Torah, also ties God's words to lying down and rising up
'when thou liest down, and when thou risest up', from JPS 1917.
the Shema and Nitnem are the same practice under two names
one honest difference: the Shema charges parents to teach; Nitnem is each Sikh's own daily discipline.

games.q: your family wants to pray together at night, but everyone's schedule is different and someone always falls asleep. what does today suggest?
o: keep it short and keep it going; the house holds the praise.
skip it until everyone can stay awake for the full set.
let each person pray alone, since together never works out.
games.why: Bebe: the hymn doesn't say everyone stays awake. it says the praise is sung in that house. even briefly counts.

practice: Close your eyes and picture the people you'd most like to end a day with, near you or far away, awake or dozing.
If you pray, you can hold them in mind as the day's last words; if not, just let them be in the room of your thoughts, together, for the sit.

wordCard.voice: Family Nitnem. Keeping some of the daily banis together at home, even briefly, even when someone dozes off.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Nitnem, the daily rule: the banis read at dawn, sunset and bedtime.

carryVoice: Pray together, even briefly, and let the house hold the praise when someone's too tired to. Goodnight, for today.
